claims.text: Depositing a thin Cr layer on Q235 steel and air annealing it at approximately 850 °C induces a continuous Fe–Cr spinel oxide layer.
The resulting Fe–Cr spinel oxide layer is self-healing.
The Fe–Cr spinel oxide layer retards corrosion of Q235 steel at room temperature relative to untreated Q235 steel.
The Fe–Cr spinel oxide layer retards corrosion of Q235 steel under aggressive salt exposure at 700–900 °C relative to untreated Q235 steel.
Pre-deposited Cr facilitates nucleation and growth of Cr-rich oxide phases during annealing.
The Cr-rich oxide phases develop into a continuous and adherent spinel layer.
At high temperature, self-healing of the spinel layer limits oxidation and salt-induced degradation.
At room temperature, the Cr-derived oxide forms a stable passivating film.
Cr-coated and annealed Q235 samples will have lower mass change than untreated Q235 during high-temperature corrosion testing.
Cr-coated and annealed Q235 samples will develop fewer microcracks than untreated Q235 during high-temperature exposure.
Cr-coated and annealed Q235 samples will exhibit less spallation than untreated Q235 during high-temperature exposure.
Cr-coated and annealed Q235 samples will possess a more uniform passivating film at room temperature than untreated Q235.
Microscopy of treated samples will reveal a continuous Fe–Cr spinel layer.
Protection requires a uniform deposited Cr layer and sufficient annealing.
Excessive substrate roughness or contamination may prevent the proposed protective mechanism.
Departures from the specified temperature, time, or salt concentration may prevent the proposed protective mechanism.
